opus-5.5.text:
I think mathematics is really the cleanest place to start if what you care about is reasoning. When we started Harmonic, the goal was always to build something that could reason at a superhuman level, and the question was where you get the signal to train that. Math is unique because it's fundamentally about reasoning in its purest form. There's no ambiguity about whether an argument is correct once you write it down formally. If you express a proof in a language like Lean, a computer can check it, and that gives you a perfect verifier. You don't need a human grader, you don't need to argue about taste or style; the proof either goes through or it doesn't.

That matters enormously for training. Reinforcement learning works best when you have a reliable reward, and with formal math you have essentially unlimited, perfectly accurate feedback. The system can attempt problems, check its own work, generate new problems, and keep improving without hitting the ceiling of human-labeled data. In most domains you eventually run out of high-quality data or you can't tell whether the model is actually right. In math, you can keep climbing.

And the second reason is that math sits underneath almost everything else. Physics, engineering, computer science, a lot of finance: they're all built on mathematical reasoning. So if you can build a system that genuinely reasons well in math, and can verify that its reasoning is correct, you've built something that transfers. Software verification is a great example: proving that code does what it's supposed to do is, in the end, a mathematical problem. So we see math not as a narrow niche, but as the training ground for general reasoning, and as a path toward AI whose outputs you can actually trust because they come with a proof attached.

r001.rationale: The response says physics and other fields are built on mathematical reasoning, but does not state that mathematics explains physical phenomena using a compact set of symbols.

r002.rationale: It describes formal proofs and Lean verification, but does not identify explicitly agreed deductive rules as the basis for shared mathematical reasoning.

r003.rationale: It says mathematical reasoning transfers to fields such as physics, engineering, computer science, and finance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that math is the one domain where you get an objectively verifiable reward signal for reasoning. If you're trying to build a system that can actually reason, you need to know when it's right, and in most domains you can't. Ask a model for a business strategy or a legal argument and the feedback is fuzzy, delayed, and often comes from a human whose judgment is itself noisy. In mathematics, if you write a proof in a formal language like Lean, a tiny trusted kernel checks it, and the answer is binary. Either the proof compiles or it doesn't. That means you can run reinforcement learning at enormous scale without worrying that the model is learning to game a soft evaluator.

The second reason is that math is the substrate under everything else. Physics, engineering, cryptography, software verification, economics, they all bottom out in mathematical structure. So if you can get a system that genuinely discovers and proves new mathematics, you aren't just solving competition problems. You're building the core reasoning engine that those other fields need. We think of formal math as the training ground where the model learns what it feels like to be rigorously correct, and then that capability transfers.

And the third thing is practical. Humans are the bottleneck in a lot of AI progress right now because we have to label data or judge outputs. In formal math the verifier is the labeler. The model can generate millions of attempts, the kernel sorts them, and the signal is perfectly clean. That loop closes without a person in it, which is the thing you need if you want a system that can keep improving past the level of its teachers. Nobody can hand-grade a proof that no human has ever seen before, but Lean can.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematics underlies fields such as physics, but does not say it explains physical phenomena using a compact set of symbols.

r002.rationale: It describes Lean’s trusted kernel checking proofs, but does not identify explicitly agreed deductive rules as the basis for shared mathematical reasoning.

r003.rationale: It says mathematical reasoning capability transfers to other fields, naming physics, engineering, cryptography, software verification, and economics.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematics is a great starting point because you can explore problems that require deep reasoning, but you also have a precise way to check whether you’re right. A proof has to hold up step by step; sounding convincing isn’t enough.

That gives you a powerful feedback loop for building an AI system. It can propose an approach, test it, find a mistake, and try again. And the problems can keep getting harder, so you’re not limited to learning a fixed set of answers.

The hope is that the capabilities you build along the way—breaking a difficult problem into smaller pieces, choosing useful abstractions, and recovering from failed approaches—will be useful beyond mathematics, too. Math gives you a clean setting in which to develop and measure those capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response describes mathematical proofs and feedback, but does not say mathematics explains physical phenomena with a compact set of symbols.

r002.rationale: It says proofs must hold up step by step, but does not identify explicitly agreed deductive rules as the basis for shared mathematical reasoning.

r003.rationale: It says mathematical capabilities may be useful beyond mathematics, but does not specify generalization to other quantitative fields.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematics is a good starting point because it combines very difficult reasoning with a very clear way to check whether you’re right. You can have a problem whose solution requires a genuinely creative idea, but once you have a proof, you can verify it rigorously. That’s a powerful combination for building an AI system: you can explore different approaches and get reliable feedback about which ones work.

It also forces you to go beyond producing something that sounds plausible. In mathematics, an argument can look convincing and still be wrong. The goal is to build a system that can work through those details, recognize when an approach fails, and try something else. Those capabilities seem useful well beyond mathematics.

r001.rationale: The response discusses mathematical reasoning and proof verification, but does not say mathematics explains physical phenomena with a compact set of symbols.

r002.rationale: It mentions rigorous proof checking, but does not identify explicitly agreed deductive rules as the basis for shared mathematical reasoning.

r003.rationale: It says the capabilities seem useful well beyond mathematics, but does not specifically hypothesize that mathematical proficiency generalizes to other quantitative fields.
